sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Fisher King is a hero of British or Arthurian legend. According to the Grail tales, a wound nearly killed him. He stays in his boat and fishes, and all the land grows withered about him. He had once been a vigorous youth. He rashly fought a rider he met, and the man left the point of a lance in his groin. Before he died, the rider had written 'The Grail' on the weapon's tip. A magic stone held him between life and death. He waited in pain for someone to break the spell. Some writers deny any Celtic link here. Others read the king through the image of the Blemished King, a figure tied to the land as if to a spouse. In that view the earth turns fruitful only while its ruler is healthy. He could not renew the earth goddess, for he lacked the healing force of the Grail. Beyond the Grail cycle, the king appears in T. S. Eliot's poem 'The Waste Land' and in the film comedy of the same name. In some versions Alain le Gros is the father of Percival. He earned the title Fisher King by feeding a crowd from a single fish, then raising the castle of Corbenic to hold the Grail. Other names for this king are Anfortas, Alain, Bron, Pelles, and Rothniam.
